Case Study Topic - Exactly-Once Event De-duplication Engine

Prepared by: Aayush Jadhav, Roll No. 18 | Mohit Kotwal, Roll No. 25 | Class: D12A | Group No.: 09

1. Project Title

Exactly-Once Event De-duplication Engine — a stream-processing middleware that detects duplicate events using event identifiers and a configurable sliding timestamp window.

2. Case Study Problem / Problem Statement

Distributed applications may receive the same message more than once because of retries, consumer restarts, network interruptions, and queue redelivery. Events can also arrive out of order or be processed by different workers. If every delivery reaches a downstream application, a logical operation such as a payment, order update, or telemetry event may be applied repeatedly. This project addresses the challenge of identifying repeated logical events consistently across multiple workers while maintaining recently seen event state in a shared key-value store.

3. Proposed Solution and Objective

The proposed system places a Deduplication Proxy between a message queue and downstream consumers. Each event carries a stable event_id, event_timestamp, event_type, and payload. The proxy validates the event and performs an atomic check-and-record operation against a shared key-value store. A configurable time window defines how long event identifiers are retained for duplicate detection. New events are recorded and forwarded; repeated events within the active window are discarded and logged. The objective is to demonstrate reliable deduplication, shared state across workers, and safe retry behaviour in a manageable student-project prototype.

4. Assigned System-Design Concept / How the Project Demonstrates It

Assigned concept: Exactly-Once Event De-duplication Engine using a sliding timestamp window. The concept is implemented in the proxy, which checks whether an event identifier has already been recorded within the configured window. A shared KV store allows all workers to consult common state. Atomic insertion prevents two workers from simultaneously treating the same event as new. The MVP demonstrates duplicate suppression within the configured window; full end-to-end exactly-once business effects also require downstream idempotency or a transaction spanning state and output, which is outside the initial prototype.

5.2 Out of Scope

The MVP will not implement a production-scale managed Kafka cluster, multi-region replication, unlimited event-history retention, an enterprise monitoring platform, or guaranteed transactional exactly-once effects across arbitrary downstream systems. A local Docker-based setup and simulated failures will be used first to reduce setup costs and integration effort. A graphical dashboard is optional; console logs and test reports are sufficient to demonstrate core behaviour.

7. Feasibility Analysis

7.1 Technical Feasibility

The project is technically feasible with Python, FastAPI, Redis, and Docker Compose. Python supports event-processing logic and automated tests; Redis provides shared key-value state and atomic operations; Redis Streams can serve as the MVP queue. Two worker processes can share the same Redis instance to demonstrate concurrency. Out-of-order delivery and failures can be generated with test scripts rather than requiring a production cloud environment. The main challenge is coordinating state recording with message acknowledgement and output delivery, so the MVP will document the boundary between duplicate suppression and end-to-end exactly-once effects.

Target / Production-style ComponentMVP Implementation / SubstituteReason it is feasible
Managed message queueRedis Streams or deterministic queue simulatorReproduces event delivery, redelivery, and out-of-order test cases locally.
Cloud KV storeLocal Redis containerProvides shared state and atomic operations without cloud cost.
Distributed worker fleetTwo local worker processes/containersDemonstrates shared-state coordination and worker failure scenarios.

7.2 Complexity Assessment

ModuleComplexity (Low/Medium/High)Reason / Main challenge
Event schema and validationLowSmall JSON schema and deterministic validation rules.
Window-based deduplicationMediumRequires a clear event-time/processing-time policy and correct expiry semantics.
Atomic state and queue integrationMediumMust prevent concurrent claims and coordinate acknowledgements/retries.

Overall feasibility: High for a controlled MVP. The core algorithm, shared state, queue integration, and test scenarios can be built using open-source tools on a student laptop. The main constraints are local deployment limits and the distinction between duplicate suppression and full end-to-end exactly-once effects. These limitations will be documented and tested.

7.3 Time Feasibility

The project is estimated to require 7–10 working days for a two-member team, provided the core engine is prioritised over a polished dashboard. The implementation plan allocates time to the event model, deduplication logic, queue/KV integration, failure tests, benchmarking, and documentation. If time is limited, a local queue simulator can be used before integrating Redis Streams.

7.4 Resource Feasibility

Required resources include a laptop, Python 3.11 or later, pip, Docker Desktop with Docker Compose, Redis, a code editor, and Git. FastAPI and testing packages are free. No paid cloud account is required for the MVP. Test inputs will be generated by scripts, including duplicate IDs, out-of-order timestamps, malformed events, and worker/KV failure scenarios.

7.5 Operational Feasibility

The demo will be started with Docker Compose and Python commands for producers and workers. A configuration file will set the deduplication window, retry limit, and queue names. Logs will show accepted events, duplicates dropped, invalid events, retries, and failures. Tests will use fixed event sequences and reset commands for repeatability. Configuration changes will require restarting the relevant process unless live reload is added.

7.6 Risk Analysis

Risk / FailureImpactMitigation / RecoveryMVP limitation (if any)
Concurrent duplicate deliveryTwo workers could both forward the same event.Use Redis atomic SET NX with expiry or a Lua script; test simultaneous submissions.Guarantee depends on state/output/ack coordination.
KV unavailable or network timeoutDuplicate status cannot be verified.Fail closed, retain/retry the queue message, and resume after Redis recovers.Availability is reduced while KV is unavailable.
Worker crash after state writeMessage may be redelivered after state is recorded.On redelivery, check shared state and suppress duplicate output; make downstream consumer idempotent.No universal exactly-once side-effect guarantee across independent systems.

10. System Architecture

The high-level architecture is shown below. The MVP uses a producer, message queue, two deduplication workers, a shared Redis KV store, a valid-event output, and a downstream consumer. Configuration and monitoring are kept separate from the event data path.

10.1 Data and Control Pathways

1. The producer creates an event with a stable event_id, event_timestamp, event_type, and payload, then publishes it to the queue.
2. The queue delivers the event to a worker; delivery may be out of order or repeated after retry.
3. The worker validates the schema and passes the event to the Deduplication Proxy. Invalid events are rejected and logged.
4. The proxy checks the shared KV store using an atomic check-and-record operation. If the ID is already present within the active window, the event is marked duplicate and not forwarded.
5. If the ID is new, the proxy records the ID and expiry/window metadata. After a successful state operation, it routes the event to the valid-event output and acknowledges the queue message.
6. The downstream consumer processes accepted events. It should be idempotent because a crash between state commit, output delivery, and queue acknowledgement can still require recovery logic.
Control path: configuration defines window duration, retry policy, and worker count; monitoring records accepted, duplicate, invalid, retry, and failure counts.

Data path: Producer → Message Queue → Deduplication Worker → Deduplication Proxy ↔ Shared Redis KV → Valid Event Output → Downstream Consumer. Control path: Configuration → Workers/Proxy; metrics and health status → logs and test report.

15. Conclusion

The proposed Exactly-Once Event De-duplication Engine is feasible as a student-team MVP. Python, Redis, and a local queue/Redis Streams setup are sufficient to demonstrate sliding-window deduplication, shared state across workers, out-of-order delivery, and failure handling without paid cloud infrastructure. Duplicate suppression at the proxy is not, by itself, a universal end-to-end exactly-once guarantee across independent storage and consumer transactions. The MVP will state this boundary clearly and use atomic state operations, retries, and idempotent downstream handling to reduce duplicate effects.
